subject: Heart failure
relation: means the heart cannot pump blood properly,
object: not that it has stopped or is about to stop; there is no cure, but treatment and lifestyle changes can help.
source_quote: Heart failure is when your heart cannot pump blood properly. It does not mean your heart has stopped working or is about to stop working. There's no cure, but treatment and lifestyle changes can help.

subject: Symptoms of heart failure
object: feeling out of breath when doing everyday activities or lying down; being more out of breath than expected when doing physical activity; feeling weak, light-headed or very tired, particularly after moving or doing physical activity; feeling light-headed or dizzy; swelling in the feet, ankles, legs or tummy, or feeling bloated; sudden weight gain; coughing at night; and coughing up frothy pink phlegm.
source_quote: Symptoms of heart failure include: feeling out of breath when doing everyday activities or lying down being more out of breath than you would expect when doing physical activity feeling weak, light-headed or very tired, particularly after moving or doing physical activity feeling light-headed or dizzy swelling in your feet, ankles, legs or tummy, or feeling bloated sudden weight gain coughing at night coughing up frothy pink phlegm

subject: Heart failure
object: suddenly, for example after a heart attack or infection, or through long-term cardiac strain from conditions such as high blood pressure or coronary heart disease.
source_quote: Causes of heart failure It can happen suddenly, such as after a heart attack or infection, or from long-term strain on your heart from high blood pressure or coronary heart disease, for example.

subject: Other possible causes of heart failure
object: heart valve disease, cardiomyopathy, rhythm problems, chronic kidney disease, anaemia, haemochromatosis causing too much iron in the blood, and thyroid problems.
source_quote: Other possible causes of heart failure include: heart valve disease cardiomyopathy heart rhythm problems chronic kidney disease anaemia haemochromatosis (a condition that leads to too much iron in your blood) thyroid problems

subject: Anyone can develop heart failure, but risk
object: people aged 65 or older, people with overweight or obesity, pregnant people, smokers, people drinking a lot of alcohol and people using cocaine.
source_quote: Anyone can get heart failure but you may be more at risk if you: are 65 or older are living with overweight or obesity are pregnant smoke drink a lot of alcohol use cocaine

subject: If a doctor suspects heart failure,
object: tests of how well the heart and lungs are working and refer the person to a cardiologist.
source_quote: If the doctor thinks you may have heart failure, they will do some tests to see how well your heart and lungs are working, and refer you to a heart specialist (cardiologist).

subject: Tests for heart failure
object: blood and urine samples, an ECG, scans such as chest X-ray or echocardiogram or MRI, and lung tests such as peak flow and spirometry; some tests may require going to hospital.
source_quote: Tests for heart failure may include: asking for samples of your blood and pee an electrocardiogram (ECG) scans such as a chest X-ray, echocardiogram and MRI scan tests to check your lungs, such as a peak flow test and spirometry You may need to go to hospital for some of these tests.

subject: Heart failure has different types and stages, and after diagnosis the doctor
object: the person's type and stage: type concerns why the heart pumps less well, while stage describes symptom severity.
source_quote: There are different types and stages of heart failure. If you're diagnosed with heart failure, your doctor will discuss the type and stage with you. The type relates to why your heart is not pumping as well as it should. The stage of heart failure explains how severe your symptoms are.

subject: Heart failure currently has no cure, but treatment
object: ease symptoms and help prevent worsening, with the treatment depending on the type and stage of heart failure and the person's overall health.
source_quote: There is currently no cure for heart failure, but treatment aims to ease symptoms and help prevent your condition from getting worse. Your treatment will depend on the type and stage of heart failure you have, and your overall health.

subject: For heart failure symptoms, different medicines
object: increase urination and reduce fluid build-up, such as the diuretic furosemide; widen blood vessels so the heart does less work pumping, such as candesartan or enalapril; and slow the heart so it needs less oxygen, such as beta blockers.
source_quote: Heart failure Medicines You may be given different types of medicine to help your symptoms. These include medicines to: make you pee more to reduce fluid build-up in your body (diuretics), such as furosemide widen your blood vessels, so your heart does not have to work as hard to pump blood (for example, candesartan or enalapril) slow your heart down, so it does not need as much oxygen (such as beta blockers)

subject: Surgery for heart failure
object: improve blood flow through blocked or damaged arteries, repair or replace damaged valves, or fit a pacemaker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator to control heart rate or correct an irregular heartbeat.
source_quote: You may need surgery if you have heart failure. This could be to: improve blood flow from blocked or damaged arteries repair or replace damaged heart valves fit a pacemaker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) to control your heart rate or fix an irregular heartbeat

subject: In severe heart failure, people
object: a left ventricular assist device to help the heart pump properly, or a heart transplant if treatments are not helping.
source_quote: If your heart failure is severe, you may be offered: a device that helps your heart pump blood properly (left ventricular assist device) a heart transplant, if treatments are not helping

subject: Everyone diagnosed with heart failure
object: cardiac rehabilitation; depending on their condition and local availability, it may include safe-exercise assessment and advice, classes or an individual exercise programme, lifestyle information and support such as healthy eating, and support groups sharing experiences; programmes may run in hospital, clinics or the community with in-person or online sessions.
source_quote: Everyone diagnosed with heart failure should be offered cardiac rehabilitation. What you're offered depends on your condition and what's available where you live but may include: an assessment and advice about how you can safely exercise exercise classes or a personal exercise programme guidance, information and support around lifestyle changes, such as healthy eating support groups and the chance to share your experiences with other people who have heart failure These programmes may take place in hospital, clinics or in the community, and involve face-to-face or online sessions.

subject: The NHS urgent advice in heart failure
relation: is to request an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 if
object: breathlessness occurs lying down or during everyday activity, frothy pink phlegm is coughed up, or weight has suddenly increased; NHS 111 can be contacted by phone or online.
source_quote: Heart failure Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appoint or get help from NHS 111 if: you feel breathless when lying down or from everyday activity you're coughing up frothy pink phlegm you have suddenly gained weight You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

subject: The NHS emergency advice for heart failure
object: severe breathing difficulty with gasping or choking or inability to speak, pale or blue or grey lips or skin that may be easier to see on palms or soles or gums in brown or black skin, or someone who has passed out and is not responding normally; do not drive yourself to A&E, and the person answering 999 will advise what to do.
source_quote: Heart failure Immediate action required: Call 999 if: you're having severe difficulty breathing – you're gasping, choking or not able to get words out your lips or skin are pale, blue or grey – on brown or black skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands, soles of the feet or gums someone has passed out and is not responding normally Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

subject: Although heart failure currently has no cure, treatment and lifestyle changes
object: control symptoms and keep heart failure stable for many years.
source_quote: While there's currently no cure, treatment and lifestyle changes can help manage symptoms and keep heart failure stable for many years.

subject: As part of heart failure treatment, referral
object: to a doctor-and-nurse palliative or symptom-control team; palliative care focuses on quality of life for anyone with a lifelong incurable illness and includes symptom management, comfort, practical needs such as home equipment, family support and end-of-life care if appropriate.
source_quote: Heart failure As part of your treatment you should be referred to a team of doctors and nurses for palliative care (symptom control team or palliative care team). Palliative care focuses on improving your quality of life and is for anyone who has a lifelong illness that cannot be cured. Palliative care treatment includes: managing your symptoms helping you feel more comfortable thinking about your practical needs, such as equipment you may need at home supporting your family end of life care, if appropriate

subject: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
object: diastolic dysfunction and often results from cardiac damage due to comorbidities such as obesity, chronic kidney disease or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or accumulation disorders such as cardiac amyloidosis.
source: Article: Castiglione V, Aimo A, Vergaro G et al. Biomarkers for the diagnosis and management of heart failure. Heart Failure Reviews 2021
source_quote: HFpEF is predominantly characterized by diastolic dysfunction and often results from heart damage due to comorbidities (e.g., obesity, chronic kidney disease (CKD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) or accumulation disorders (e.g., cardiac amyloidosis).

subject: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
object: systolic dysfunction secondary to direct cardiac damage such as an acute coronary syndrome, a cardiomyopathy or valve disease.
source: Article: Castiglione V, Aimo A, Vergaro G et al. Biomarkers for the diagnosis and management of heart failure. Heart Failure Reviews 2021
source_quote: HFrEF, on the other hand, is characterized prevalently by systolic dysfunction, secondary to a direct heart damage (such as an acute coronary syndrome), a cardiomyopathy or a valve disease .

subject: Although preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure likely has multifactorial pathophysiology, reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure
object: cardiovascular neuroendocrine systems: sympathetic and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation is not adequately opposed by increased natriuretic-peptide release, promoting progressive chamber hypertrophy and dilatation that impair pumping, cause symptoms and increase susceptibility to arrhythmias and conduction disorders.
source: Article: Castiglione V, Aimo A, Vergaro G et al. Biomarkers for the diagnosis and management of heart failure. Heart Failure Reviews 2021
source_quote: While the pathophysiology of HFpEF is likely multifactorial, an imbalance in the neuroendocrine systems regulating cardiovascular homeostasis plays a central role in HFrEF. The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) are overactivated and are not adequately counterbalanced by the increased release of natriuretic peptides (NPs). This imbalance promotes structural alterations leading to progressive hypertrophy and dilation of cardiac chambers. These alterations have detrimental effects on cardiac pump function, and ultimately lead to symptom development, as well as an increased susceptibility to arrhythmias and cardiac conduction disorders .

subject: BNP
relation: is produced primarily by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to
object: volume or pressure overload; circulating BNP and NT-proBNP are normally very low but increase significantly in heart failure as a mechanism to restore normal haemodynamics.
source: Article: Castiglione V, Aimo A, Vergaro G et al. Biomarkers for the diagnosis and management of heart failure. Heart Failure Reviews 2021
source_quote: BNP is produced primarily by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to volume or pressure overload . Circulating BNP and NT-proBNP levels are normally very low, but increase significantly in HF patients as a mechanism to restore normal hemodynamics.

subject: In older adults, reduced exercise tolerance
object: normal physiological ageing or noncardiac causes, and comorbidities can mimic heart-failure signs and complicate diagnosis; older people with preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure may lack classic symptoms and have subtle presentations.
source: Article: Upadhya B, Kitzman DW. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: New approaches to diagnosis and management. Clinical Cardiology 2019
source_quote: However, symptoms of reduced exercise tolerance are common in the older adults and have been shown to reflect normal physiological changes related to aging or could be related to non‐cardiac etiologies. Furthermore, the diagnosis of HF in the older patients may be difficult due to the presence of co‐morbidities, some of which can mimic HF signs and further confound the diagnosis of HF. In addition, older patients with HFpEF may not present with “classic” HF symptoms and may instead have very subtle clinical presentations.

subject: Up to one-third of outpatients with preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure
object: BNP below typical diagnostic thresholds, which can challenge using BNP to diagnose heart failure.
source: Article: Upadhya B, Kitzman DW. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: New approaches to diagnosis and management. Clinical Cardiology 2019
source_quote: Up to one‐third of HFpEF outpatients may have a B‐type natriuretic peptide (BNP) level that is below the typical diagnostic thresholds. This can challenge the common practice of using BNP to make HF diagnosis.

subject: Renal disease in heart failure
object: heart failure can cause chronic kidney disease through increased venous pressure and low cardiac output causing renal hypoperfusion, inflammation and sympathetic activation; conversely, renal dysfunction may worsen heart failure through sodium and fluid retention, accelerated atherosclerosis, inflammation, anaemia, uraemic toxins and neurohormonal activation.
source: Article: Lam CSP, Chandramouli C, Ahooja V et al. SGLT ‐2 Inhibitors in Heart Failure: Current Management, Unmet Needs, and Therapeutic Prospects. Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease 2019
source_quote: 42 The pathophysiology of renal disease in HF is complex: HF can lead to CKD through increased venous pressure and low cardiac output resulting in renal hypoperfusion, inflammation, and sympathetic activation. Conversely, kidney dysfunction may worsen HF through increased sodium and fluid retention, accelerated atherosclerosis, inflammation, anemia, uremic toxins, and neurohormonal activation.

subject: Even symptomatic heart failure
relation: can be difficult to diagnose and treat early because of
object: poor public awareness and suboptimal nonspecialist diagnosis with potentially limited access to tests such as echocardiography; its variable presentation includes breathlessness and exercise intolerance overlapping with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, anaemia and diabetes.
source: Article: Lam CSP, Chandramouli C, Ahooja V et al. SGLT ‐2 Inhibitors in Heart Failure: Current Management, Unmet Needs, and Therapeutic Prospects. Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease 2019
source_quote: Even with symptomatic disease, major barriers to early diagnosis and treatment of HF remain, such as poor awareness of the disease among the general population 10, 11, 12, 13 and suboptimal diagnosis by nonspecialist healthcare practitioners, who may have limited access to diagnostic tools such as echocardiography. 14, 15 This is of particular concern in view of the variable clinical presentation of HF, 16 as well as the overlap of symptoms (eg, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance) of the condition with common comorbidities, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease (CKD), anemia, and diabetes mellitus.
